annotations.annotation_text: Page 338 opens Book 2, Chapter 3 ("The Tavern") during the Age of Heroes phase. This passage continues HCE behind the bar at his Chapelizod pub, the Norwegian Captain tale, the television broadcast, the twelve customers drinking and judging, featuring HCE, the Twelve Customers, Butt and Taff. The nocturnal dream-narrative layers Dublin topography, world mythology, and linguistic alchemy into polysemic prose.
sources: Campbell, Joseph and Robinson, Henry Morton. A Skeleton Key to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/skeletonkeytofin00camp
McHugh, Roland. Annotations to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/annotationstofin0000mchu_h5g8
Gordon, John. Finnegans Wake: A Plot Summary. https://johngordonfinnegan.weebly.com
JJDA: Finnegans Wake Genetic Edition. https://jjda.ie

annotations.annotation_text: The Buckley parable (338.05): an anecdote celebrated by Joyce's father. Irish private Buckley spots a decorated Russian General defecating in a battlefield trench and prepares to shoot him.
sources: FinnegansWeb: Buckley and the Russian General. https://www.finnegansweb.com

annotations.annotation_text: Moral hesitation (338.15): Buckley initially pities the vulnerable general in his exposed, helpless posture of excretion, but compassion turns to fury when he witnesses the general desecrate the soil.

Mid-page polysemic node on page 338 ("The Tavern"): Joyce weaves multilingual puns across 60+ languages — etymological roots from the Contemporary Literature Press lexicons (Romanian, Scandinavian, Slavic, Classical) intersect with local Dublin speech rhythms. The Age of Heroes dream-logic transforms ordinary syntax into a palimpsest of global literary and mythic references.
sources: Tindall, William York. A Reader's Guide to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/readersguidetofi00tind
Contemporary Literature Press: Multilingual Lexicons for FW. https://editura.mttlc.ro
Atherton, James S. The Books at the Wake. https://archive.org/details/booksatwake0000athe

annotations.annotation_text: The insult to the sod (338.25): the general wipes his backside with a fresh clump of green grass/sod. The green sod symbolizes Ireland, triggering Buckley's patriotic fury at imperial desecration.
sources: Atherton, James S. The Books at the Wake. https://archive.org/details/booksatwake0000athe

annotations.annotation_text: The Oedipal shot (338.32): Buckley fires, shooting the general in the buttocks. In Freudian and Viconian terms, this represents the rising son overthrowing and castrating the oppressive patriarchal authority.
sources: Bishop, John. Joyce's Book of the Dark. https://archive.org/details/joycesbookofdark0000bish
